C001035.text:
In Maine, toxic "forever chemicals" known as PFAS were present in wastewater sludge spread decades ago as fertilizer. Farmers were told this fertilizer was safe to use and using it would help their local municipalities. Instead, these toxic chemicals devastated some of our family farmers and rendered farm land and products unusable.

The University of Maine is now a leader in research on how to address and remove PFAS, and it is critical the federal government continue to support this work. I've secured nearly $33 million through the Agriculture Appropriations bill over the past five years for the Agricultural Research Service at the University of Maine to establish a new Center of Excellence for PFAS Solutions, and will continue working to help farmers who are facing the consequences of PFAS contamination through no fault of their own.

I sent a letter last month opposing the closures of two Taxpayer Assistance Centers—one in Bangor, Maine, and one in Augusta, Maine.

This week, the new federal funding bill for agriculture, rural development and the FDA was introduced and briefly debated, as the ranking member of the subcommittee, I raised my concerns and hope that they can be addressed as we negotiate further on this bill.

It is hard to make America healthy again when this bill takes fruit and vegetables from over 5 million women, infants, and children and eliminates the Healthy Food Financing Initiative. When ag producers and rural communities are struggling with skyrocketing costs over the past year, this bill is cutting staff and programs on which they rely at the Farm Service Agency, Rural Development and NRCS.

This bill makes it harder for rural communities to have clean water and affordable utilities, and it unfortunately retreats from investment in our rural businesses. Lastly, the majority is offering caustic riders that simply take the focus away from agriculture and the real challenges we face.

Rural America needs help now more than ever and I hope that we can improve this bill as the appropriations process continues.

On Tuesday, the House Appropriations Committee voted on the Fiscal Year 2027 Military Construction, Veterans Affairs, and Related Agencies funding bill. I supported this bipartisan funding bill because of its strong efforts to provide for military readiness through access to safe housing, childcare, and strong, resilient military installations.

However, there are a few areas where I feel that the bill falls short in providing for our servicemembers, veterans, and their families. Access to quality healthcare is one of the most important ways we can support members of the armed forces. This bill does not do enough to give veterans access to the timely healthcare that they deserve, and it lacks the accountability needed to make sure that taxpayers’ dollars are being spent responsibly.

I look forward to working with my colleagues on both sides of the aisle to produce a final bill that best supports the needs of our veteran and military communities.

RT by @RepRickCrawford: Arkansas Representative and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rick Crawford is advocating in Washington for the controversial reauthorization of FISA - the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act.

Here's what he had to say in our interview with him today.

In the current heightened threat environment, with U.S. military operations in Iran, the CCP looking to fill power vacuums around the world, and terrorist proxies plotting attacks on Americans and U.S. interests, Congress cannot take this critical national security tool away from President Trump. RISAA, passed by Congress in 2024, was the largest FBI and FISA reform in decades, with 56 reform mandates to address past abuses of the FISA 702 tool and gaps. Today’s 702 is a very different one from when Congress voted in 2024.

With this legislative proposal, Congress is building on these reforms by making real enhancements to privacy protections for Americans, increasing accountability for abuses, and providing for a first-ever external review for the primary source of past abuses – the FBI.

It’s been made abundantly clear that no option will be 100% perfect in the eyes of everyone, but this bill makes measurable reforms to strengthen accountability and safeguards, while maintaining the criticality of the national security tool. 

At this point in the debate, many in Congress understand the significant advantage 702 provides U.S. national security, and the fervent need to protect Americans’ privacy and civil liberties. We should not sacrifice one for the other, and this revised legislation strikes that balance

This morning, I joined Mayor Dr. Victor Treviño, State Rep. Richard Raymond, @cityoflaredo Council members, and community partners for a press conference at the Laredo Water Museum to highlight federal investments strengthening our water infrastructure and long term reliability.

As Laredo faces ongoing drought, rising demand, and pressure on the Rio Grande, we’re advancing solutions to diversify and secure our water sources. I helped secure $20 million in federal funding for key infrastructure improvements, including interconnecting major treatment plants to improve system redundancy, flexibility, and emergency response. Additional support includes authorization to dredge Lake Casa Blanca to expand storage capacity and improve water quality, along with major water line replacement projects modernizing more than 80,000 linear feet of pipeline to reduce system failures and support continued growth. These coordinated efforts have strengthened system performance and helped Laredo achieve a full year without boil water notices in 2025.

I also provided an update on tariff reimbursements and the need to ensure the process is transparent and fair. When I first ran for State Representative back in 1992, my aspiration was to represent my hometown of Tarkio, Missouri. I was a twenty-seven year old farmer who just wanted to stand up for a way of life and his community.  I never could have imagined where that decision would take me.   

For 8 years in the Missouri House and Senate, I fought for Northwest Missourians. From deregulating vehicle inspections, to standing for chain gangs, to securing funding for rural schools in the desegregation fight, I never lost sight of why I was sent to Jefferson City. Then, in 2000, the good, hardworking people of Missouri’s Sixth District entrusted me to be their voice in Congress.    

For 26 years, I have had the privilege of serving, culminating in becoming the Chairman of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and passing some of the most significant legislation in our nation’s history.  The responsibility entrusted to me is not something I have ever taken for granted. Not for a single day.   

What I’m most proud of is the work my team did when Washington made life harder for the people of Missouri’s Sixth. Together, we stood with hundreds of thousands of Missourians in their toughest moments.  We helped them cut through red tape and navigate a system that often felt stacked against them.  We got them answers and fought to deliver real results when they needed them most.   

I’ve said all of that to say this: After considerable reflection, 2026 will be my final year in Congress.  This wasn’t an easy decision, but it’s the right one. I believe in making room for the next generation. It’s time to pass the torch and allow a new guard of conservative leaders to step forward and chart a path forward for Missourians.    

That doesn’t mean I’m slowing down, not even close.  As I enter the 4th quarter of my life, I have more left in me. As many of you know, I don't let grass grow under my feet. We’ve still got a lot of work to do. I’m going to fight to protect Missouri interests as we work to shape this year’s Highway Bill. I plan to finish this last term the same way I started, full speed ahead.   

Maintaining our strong democratic republic will always depend on good people stepping up to serve from every corner of our great nation. I’m grateful for my colleagues in both parties, for the people I’ve worked alongside, and even for the opponents who challenged me and made me better. Public service isn’t easy. It takes hard work, humility, a thick skin, and a willingness to fight for what’s right.   

At the end of the day, I’m still the farmer from Northwest Missouri. You’ll find me back home on the farm nearly every weekend, after all, it is planting season. In fact, I’ll probably be on a tractor this weekend. And come Monday, I’ll be heading back through Kansas City on my way to D.C. to keep doing the job you sent me there to do.   From the bottom of my heart, thank you.    

It has been the honor of a lifetime.

This is particularly important in our underserved communities, where the lack of shade trees can leave residents exposed to extreme heat, especially as climate change drives longer and more intense heatwaves.
 
The Neighborhood Tree Act will address this gap by giving local governments the federal support they need to plant and care for trees where they are needed most. It's a simple idea with real impact.

Today, with the announcement that the first two Arctic Security Cutters will be homeported in Alaska, it is becoming real. This news marks a turning point in America’s investment in the Arctic and will allow us to reassert our influence in the region—enhancing maritime commerce, strengthening cooperation with our allies, increasing deterrence against our adversaries, and ensuring our military can respond to emergencies in any environment. 

I want to commend President Donald Trump for his commitment to these critical assets. When he came into office in 2016, one of my first conversations with him focused on the importance of investing in our infrastructure so we could compete in the Arctic in the 21st century. He listened and came through on his commitment to expanding our icebreaker capacity, and I appreciate his continued dedication to this issue. 

The work is just beginning. As we move to designate Alaska’s new homeport locations, ensuring these ASCs are ready to serve will require significant shoreside infrastructure with new housing to support both the vessels and the influx of personnel. While there is a long road ahead, this announcement means new investment, new jobs, and new opportunities flowing into our communities. Today is a good day for America, a good day for the Arctic, and a good day for Alaska.

My mother spent 35 years working as a public school teacher. My father worked as an engineer. They instilled in my brothers and me a deep belief in hard work, public service, and giving back to the country that welcomed them.

I am a product of that American story. I attended California’s public schools from kindergarten through medical school, became a doctor, and now have the privilege of serving our nation in Congress. That is what the American Dream looks like.

The comments shared by President Trump are offensive, ignorant, and beneath the dignity of the office he holds. They reflect a fundamental misunderstanding of who we are as a nation. America has always been strengthened by generations of immigrants who come here, work hard, and contribute to our country. They do not weaken America — they strengthen it.

America was built by people from all over the world who believed in its promise and worked tirelessly to make it better for the next generation. That’s the story of my family, and it’s the story of millions of families across our nation.

President Trump, who was born into wealth and privilege, has never had to struggle the way so many immigrant families have. He does not understand the grit, sacrifice, and determination it takes to build a life from the ground up. This week, I am proud to recognize a dear friend, trusted partner, and remarkable leader who has dedicated her career to one of the most meaningful missions there is: helping families find the security, dignity, and hope that come with a home of their own—the remarkable Florence Kawoczka.

For the past 15 years, Florence has served as the CEO and Executive Director of Habitat for Humanity of Bucks County, leading with compassion and a clear understanding that housing is never just about walls and windows. It is about stability, opportunity, and giving families the foundation they need to build the next chapter of their lives.

I have been honored to work alongside Florence in this mission and see firsthand just how much of herself she poured into every facet of this vocation. 

Under her leadership, Habitat Bucks has grown its reach and deepened its impact in every corner of our community—partnering with more than 50 new homeowners, repairing more than 400 homes, expanding their ReStore initiatives, establishing the Almost Home financial empowerment program, and pioneering a Permanent Workforce Housing model that will keep homeownership within reach for generations of Bucks County families.

Her impact cannot be captured by numbers alone, however. It is found in the families who finally have a place to call their own, the neighborhoods made stronger, and the hope restored one home, one repair, and one act of service at a time.

As Florence prepares to retire this summer, please join me in thanking and celebrating her extraordinary leadership. She is a true agent of change.  

Florence, my friend—thank you for your partnership, service, and countless ways you have given your time, spirit, and heart to the people of our community. Congratulations on this well-earned next chapter with Paul and your family. 

For the homes she helped build, the lives she helped change, and the foundation of hope she leaves behind, Florence Kawoczka will always be a true Hometown Hero.

Putin is not only trying to seize Ukrainian land. He is trying to erase Ukrainian identity—targeting churches, synagogues, mosques, clergy, and faith communities across Ukraine.

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, more than 600 religious sites have been damaged or destroyed, and more than 50 Ukrainian clergy members have been killed. In Russian-occupied territories, religious communities that refuse to submit to Kremlin control have faced raids, detention, forced re-registration, criminal prosecution, and systematic intimidation.

These are not isolated abuses. They are part of a deliberate campaign of repression, and demand a response.

Today, I introduced the Countering Russia’s War on Faith Act to ensure Russia’s persecution of religious communities in Ukraine and Russian-occupied territories is fully documented, exposed, and met with real consequences. My legislation requires the Departments of State and Defense to jointly report on these abuses and identify those responsible for sanctionable actions.

The American Coalition for Ukraine has been a critical partner in this effort, including PA-1 constituent advocates Lauren Henasey, Ihor Chernik, and Olga Mykhaylyuk. We met this week to continue our work together on confronting this persecution directly and ensuring Russia’s assault on religious freedom does not go unanswered. Together, we will keep standing with Ukraine, defending religious freedom, and holding Russia accountable.

The irony of posting about Earth Day just a week after we lost a vote to save the Boundary Waters isn’t lost on me. It’s a tough loss that we’re still processing. But today, of all days, should remind us why these special places are worth fighting for.
 
The Boundary Waters have some of the cleanest water that you will find anywhere in this country. Endless lakes and streams filled with bass and pike and trout. Completely untouched nature and only accessible via canoe.

Allowing this copper-sulfide mine in the headwaters of the BWCA will threaten all of that, but the fight isn’t over. It looks different, yes, but the mission is still fundamentally the same: These waters are the birthright of every single one of us, and it’s our job to protect them from the corporate greed of Antofagasta. Not this mine. Not this place.
 
This coalition of Tribal Nations, outdoorsmen, conservationists, public lands enthusiasts and just your average Minnesotans who have been lucky enough to visit this place will still fight against this mine.

And anyone who is feeling defeated should look at the comments on Pete Stauber’s posts last week to get a sense of just how mad we are and how hard we are going to continue fighting.

Because the Boundary Waters have such special meaning. It’s a sacred place, and we will never stop defending it.

INTRODUCING: The Restoring Law and Order on America's Streets Act.

This legislation expands the DOJ's civil commitment authority and restores public order. 

Under current law, the DOJ can seek civil commitment for sexually dangerous people. Our bill expands this authority to include any person who poses a danger to public safety.

A danger to public safety means anyone with a serious mental illness or disorder making it seriously difficult to refrain from:

❌ Violent crime
❌ Burglary, robbery, or larceny
❌ Illegal narcotics distribution in public spaces
❌ Urban camping or squatting
❌ Vandalism

This bill also requires mandatory DOJ evaluations of homeless individuals in custody to determine whether they are a danger to public safety or a sexually dangerous person, eligible for civil commitment.

This builds directly on President Trump's Executive Order 14321, Ending Crime and Disorder on America's Streets.

Soft-on-crime policies have consequences. Law and order means something and it is time Washington started governing like it.

RT by @RepPatFallon: If you’d told me a few years ago this is where we’d be on Iran, I’d have said you were high:

1. Nuke program set back years. Enrichment and reprocessing gutted, weaponization sites destroyed, Fordow inoperable, Natanz in ruins, a generation of senior nuclear scientists eliminated.

2. Ballistic missile program crippled. Monthly production down from 100 to near zero. Roughly half the regime’s missiles and launchers destroyed. The IRGC Aerospace Force commander who ran the missile enterprise dead.

3. Air defenses devastated. American and Israeli airpower dominating Iranian skies, with strike aircraft operating over the country with near impunity.

4. Full economic warfare. Not just OFAC sanctions anymore, but military pressure layered on top: naval blockade, near-zero oil exports, choked imports, wrecked steel and petrochemical sectors, triple-digit inflation, and a currency that is effectively worthless.

5. Regime decapitation. Khamenei dead. Larijani dead. Hundreds of senior IRGC, intelligence, military, and Basij commanders dead including the IRGC commander-in-chief, the armed forces chief of staff, and the Aerospace Force commander. Mojtaba Khamenei inheriting a hollowed-out regime with no supreme authority and a gutted command structure.

6. The region turning on Tehran. Gulf states shutting down the sanctions-busting, money-laundering, and financial escape routes the regime has relied on for years. No Arab capital willing to throw Iran a lifeline. China and Russia providing limited support.

7. Proxy network shattered. Hezbollah and Hamas heavily degraded. Houthi political leadership taking direct Israeli strikes. The “Axis of Resistance” and “ring of fire” are now more slogans than real threats.

8. Syrian corridor severed. Assad is gone. The new government in Damascus is actively blocking Iranian arms transfers to Hezbollah: arresting smugglers and publicly declaring Syria will no longer serve as a transit corridor for Tehran’s terrorists. The land bridge to the Mediterranean that took decades to build is effectively closed. 

9. Lebanon pivoting west. With Hezbollah battered and resupply choked, Israel and Lebanon have opened direct peace talks for the first time since 1983, aimed at a permanent agreement and Hezbollah’s disarmament. Beirut now asserting that the Lebanese armed forces alone are responsible for national defense. This is a direct repudiation of Hezbollah’s “resistance” claim. TBD.

10. Deterrence exposed as a bluff. Four direct attacks on Israel — April 2024, October 2024, June 2025, March 2026 — failed to impose strategic cost and instead triggered heavy retaliation. Iran couldn’t even use Syria as a launchpad.

11.Economy hollowed out from within. Power shortages, water crises, factory shutdowns, pension unrest, and mass protests. Nationwide demonstrations erupted in December 2025 after a year of economic freefall, with bazaaris, oil workers, and truckers, the regime’s traditional support base, joining strikes across all 31 provinces. Running out of oil storage space. Fuel shortages. The worst crisis since 1979.

12. Scientific and technical brain drain. Beyond the nuclear experts, Iran has lost a generation of irreplaceable expertise in missile design, centrifuge engineering, and weapons development. The survivors are harder to recruit and easier to deter.

13. Naval power decimated. The regular navy shattered, IRGC navy taking growing losses as CENTCOM moves to reopen Hormuz.

And against all of this: the regime forced to play its Hormuz card at its weakest possible moment when the U.S. has options instead of when we didn’t: namely, Tehran with nuclear-armed ICBMs, 10,000 ballistic missiles, a Chinese- and Russian-built military, hundreds of thousands of attack drones, a fully operational terror network, and hundreds of billions of dollars to harden its economy.

That’s the strategic picture. It’s extraordinary. Much more to do but I can’t comprehend how much has been achieved.

I will keep working to free the Armenian prisoners, end military aid to Azerbaijan, and ensure future generations learn the truth about what happened 111 years ago.

111 years ago, 1.5 million Armenians were arrested, exiled, and killed at the hands of the Ottoman Empire. It was a genocide that is still denied by some to this day. 

That denialism manifests today, where we are continuing to see persecution and attacks on Armenian communities. I will always stand with the Armenian community in their efforts for peace and safety around the world.

This is an attack on working people, and completely unfair. I’m fighting to make housing, healthcare and education more affordable, and to undo Trump’s giveaways to the ultra-rich.

H001100.text:
Met with members of the National Beer Wholesalers Association and distributors serving Colorado’s Third District to discuss what it takes to keep businesses strong across #CO03.

Appreciate the conversation with Michael Cadez and Jerome Santiago of Central Distributing in Clifton. This is a locally rooted operation supporting jobs, investing in the community, and helping keep our regional economy moving.
We talked about keeping tax rules in place that help small businesses grow, making sure states—not Washington—stay in charge of alcohol laws, and pushing for clear, upfront pricing in healthcare so businesses and consumers know what they’re paying before they get the bill.

Small businesses in Western and Southern Colorado need certainty, not more red tape. My focus is making sure federal policy backs job creators and keeps our local economies competitive. #MesaCounty

On my way to the House floor, I had the chance to connect with Trustees from the Town of Silt, including Mayor Pro-Tem Derek Hanrahan and Town Manager Jim Mann.

We had a detailed conversation about infrastructure priorities in Silt, such as the planned non-motorized pedestrian bridge over Interstate-70 that will improve safety and connectivity for residents moving between parts of the community. We also discussed the broader role federal support can play in helping small towns move projects like this forward, along with the importance of protecting Shoshone water rights — which are critical to maintaining consistent flows through Glenwood Canyon and supporting agriculture, recreation, and local economies across the Western Slope.

These are the kinds of conversations that shape how I approach the work in Washington, grounded in real projects, real needs, and making sure communities like Silt have a strong voice in the decisions that affect them. #CO03 #GarfieldCounty

One step closer to delivering reliable water solutions for Southwest Colorado.

Yesterday, H.R. 5911, the Crystal Reservoir Conveyance Act, passed through the House Natural Resources Committee. This legislation transfers Crystal Reservoir to the City of Ouray, giving local leaders the ability to repair critical infrastructure, restore water access, and better support agriculture, wildfire response, and recreation across the region.

Water is foundational to communities across #CO03. This is a practical step to put decision-making back in local hands, reduce federal barriers, and ensure this resource is managed by the people who depend on it every day.

Appreciate the support of Chairman Westerman to advance this bill. We’ll keep pushing to get it across the finish line. #OurayCounty

Spent time this weekend in Mesa County with Club 20 sharing what I’ve learned so far in Congress—and how those new experiences now shape the way I approach this job.

One thing has become clear: the best policy comes from listening to the people back home and staying focused on practical solutions that actually work in rural communities. That means cutting through the noise in Washington and making sure the priorities of Western and Southern Colorado are what drive decisions.

I also talked through the Community Project Funding I’ve secured for #CO03 this year. In total, we delivered over $11 million for projects across Colorado’s Third District, with $3.19 million going directly to projects in Mesa County.

Those investments include funding for infrastructure improvements, water systems, and public safety projects that support continued growth in Grand Junction and the surrounding communities.

This is what effective representation looks like, bringing federal resources back home in a way that strengthens local communities and supports long-term growth across the district. #MesaCounty

Met with leaders from the Colorado Association of School Executives, including Alamosa Superintendent Diana Jones, to hear directly what schools are facing across the state.

The message was consistent. School leaders are dealing with tight budgets, workforce shortages, and the challenge of attracting and retaining teachers, especially in rural communities.

Strong schools are at the center of every community, but they cannot succeed without stable funding and a workforce pipeline that reflects the realities on the ground. My focus is making sure federal policy supports those needs and keeps opportunities within reach for families across #CO03.

E000300.text:
Colorado Democrats are at it again — taking money straight out of YOUR pocket.

A new proposal from the state legislature would cost taxpayers $7,381 in TABOR refunds — money that rightfully belongs to Colorado families.

And here’s the kicker:
75% of that money isn’t even guaranteed to go to education.

Instead, it gets dumped into a general fund  pile for politicians to spend however they want.

Let that sink in.

This is a massive redirect of taxpayer dollars with no real accountability.

Hardworking Coloradans are already struggling with rising costs, and now state Democrats want to take even more — with no guarantee of where it goes.

This is exactly why TABOR exists: to protect taxpayers from this kind of government overreach.

Colorado families deserve transparency, accountability, and to keep more of their hard-earned money — not less.
